deep.reconstruction:
PART A: 'Supplement to the method of computing precession' (Polaris, data for 1755 and 1815)

Notation. Let α, δ be the right ascension and declination at epoch 1 (1755), and α', δ' those at epoch 2 (1815). Polar distances are π = 90°−δ and π' = 90°−δ'.

Step 1: auxiliary angles p and q.
- tan p = tan½(α'−α)·cos½(δ'+δ)/sin½(δ'−δ)
- tan q = tan½(α'+α)·sin½(δ'−δ)/cos½(δ'+δ)

Step 2: the unknowns M, N, u, u'. They follow from eight equations, four per epoch.
- sinM sin u = sin½π sin½(p−q+α)
- sinN cos u = sin½π cos½(p−q+α)
- cosN cos u = cos½π sin½(p−q−α)
- cosM sin u = cos½π cos½(p−q−α)
- The primed set is the same with π', u', α' and p+q in place of p−q.
- As written, the 4th left equation has cos½(p−q+α). Gauss's own numbers use p−q−α. The sign under the '+' is underlined in the manuscript, apparently as a correction.

Modern meaning (my interpretation, not written by Gauss).
- Put φ = p−q at the first epoch and φ = p+q at the second.
- The unit 4-vector (sin½π sin½(φ+α), sin½π cos½(φ+α), cos½π sin½(φ−α), cos½π cos½(φ−α)) is a spinor / Euler–Rodrigues (Cayley–Klein) representative of the star's position. φ is a free phase.
- The equations say this vector equals sin u·(sinM,0,0,cosM) + cos u·(0,sinN,cosN,0). That is, it moves on a fixed great circle of S³ with arc parameter u.
- A great circle traced uniformly in u corresponds to a uniform rotation of the sphere by angle 2u about a fixed axis.
- Solving the generator equations, this axis lies in a fixed meridian (the solstitial colure, RA≈270°, i.e. towards the ecliptic pole) at polar distance N−M.
- So p and q are the phase choices that make both epochs lie on such a circle. The model is: Polaris, in mean-of-date coordinates, rotates uniformly about an axis near the ecliptic pole, with u linear in time.

Step 3: data.
- α = 10°55'34.380", δ = 87°59'41.12" (1755).
- α' = 13°57'7.656", δ' = 88°19'17.21" (1815).
- ½(α'+α) = 12°26'21.018"; ½(α'−α) = 1°30'46.638".
- ½(δ'+δ) = 88°9'29.165"; ½(δ'−δ) = 9'48.045".
- log cos½(δ'+δ) = 8.5070683; log sin½(δ'−δ) = 7.4549848; their difference is 1.0520835.
- log tan½(α'−α) = 8.4218043, so log tan p = 9.4738878 and p = 16°34'55.922".
- log tan½(α'+α) = 9.3435683, so log tan q = 8.2914848 and q = 1°7'15.102".

Step 4: half-angles.
- ½(p−q+α) = 13°11'37.60" and ½(p+q+α') = 15°49'39.34".
- ½π = 1°0'9.44" and ½π' = 0°50'21.395".
- ½(p−q−α) = 2°16'3.22" and ½(p+q−α') = 1°52'31.684".

Step 5: logarithms of the needed sines and cosines.
- Epoch 1: 9.3584015, 8.2429925, 9.9883822, 8.5973230, 9.9999335, 9.9996598.
- Epoch 2: 9.4357546, 8.1657669, 9.9832142, 8.5149094, 9.9999534, 9.9997673.
- These give the right-hand sides:
  - log sinM sin u = 7.6013940 and log sinM sin u' = 7.6015215.
  - log cosM sin u = 9.9995933 and log cosM sin u' = 9.9997207.
  - log sinN cos u = 8.2313747 and log sinN cos u' = 8.1489811.
  - log cosN cos u = 8.5972565 and log cosN cos u' = 8.5148628.

Step 6: solving.
- log tan M = 7.6018007 from both epochs (the consistency check works). So M = 0°13'44.5623", log cos M = 9.9999965, log sin M = 7.6017973.
- log tan N = 9.6341182 from both epochs. So N = 23°17'55.7845", log sin N = 9.5971758, log cos N = 9.9630576.
- log sin u = 9.9995967½ and log sin u' = 9.9997242.
- log cos u = 8.6341989, computed both ways; log cos u' = 8.5518052(.5).
- Hence u = 87°31'52.9335" and u' = 87°57'29.4086".
- 'Motus in 60 annis': u'−u = 25'36.4751". This corresponds to a rotation of 2×25'36.5" = 51.2"/yr.

Step 7: check for 1785.
- Interpolating linearly, u(1785) = 87°44'41.17105".
- Products:
  - sinM sin u gives 7.6014608.
  - sinN cos u gives 8.1921320.
  - cosN cos u gives 8.5580138.
  - cosM sin u gives 9.9996600.
- tan½A = 10^(7.6014608−8.1921320), so ½A = 14°23'37.99".
- tan½B = 10^(8.5580138−9.9996600), so ½B = 2°4'17.44".
- α = ½A−½B = 12°19'20.55". Gauss notes 'Bessel hat 12°19'19.44"'.
- log sin½π = 8.1921320−9.9861488 = 8.2059832. The check log cos½π = 9.9996600−9.9997161 = 9.9999439.
- Hence 90°−½π = 89°4'45.43" and δ = 88°9'30.86". Bessel has 88°9'30.91".

Step 8: epoch of closest approach to the pole.
- Closest approach is when u = 90°.
- Remaining arc: 90°−u' = 2°2'30.5914" = 7350.5914".
- t = 7350.5914/1536.4751 × 60 yr; log 441035.484 = 5.6444735, log 1536.4751 = 3.1865255, giving 287.0437 yr.
- 1815 + 287.0437 = 'Anno 2102 Jan 18'.
- At u = 90° the 4-vector is (sinM,0,0,cosM), so the minimal polar distance is π_min = 2M ≈ 27'29". This follows from the formulas but is not written on the page (my addition).

PART B: Fundamental theorem for biquadratic residues.
- Statement: Dec.[(A+Bi)/(a+bi)] − Dec.[(a+bi)/(A+Bi)] = ½(A−1)b + ½(a−1)B + ½Bb (mod 4).
- Here a, A are odd and b, B even, as in the following index tables. 'Dec.' denotes Gauss's biquadratic character index k, with (A+Bi)^{(N(a+bi)−1)/4} ≡ i^k.
- For primary numbers (a+b ≡ 1 mod 4), the right side reduces to bB/2 mod 4. This is the standard law [α/β]=[β/α](−1)^{(Nα−1)/4·(Nβ−1)/4}.
- The extra terms make the formula invariant under replacing a+bi by −(a+bi), so it covers both signs.
errors: The 4th left equation is written cos M·sin u = cos½π·cos½(p−q+α). Gauss's own computation (9.9999335+9.9996598=9.9995933) uses cos½(p−q−α), so the '+' is a slip; it is underlined, probably flagged by Gauss himself.
The date: 1815+287.0437 = 2102.044, i.e. about Jan 16–17 if 1815.0 = Jan 0, or about Jan 18 if counted from Jan 1. This is a marginal convention difference, not an error.

The 1785 RA differs from Bessel's by 1.1". This is consistent with modeling only two epochs (proper motion/nonuniformity absorbed); it is not a computational error. All other logarithmic arithmetic checked agrees to the last unit.

results.what: Fitting the motion of a star between two epochs as a uniform rotation, using half-angle (spinor/Euler–Rodrigues) coordinates. The star's 4-vector moves on a great circle of S³ with parameter u linear in time; p and q fix the phases. Used to interpolate Polaris for 1785.
results.modern_name: Cayley–Klein / Euler–Rodrigues (quaternion) parametrization of rotations; rigorous precession reduction
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1770s), Rodrigues (1840), Hamilton (1843), Cayley/Klein; rigorous precession formulas to Bessel and Gauss

results.what: Prediction of the epoch of Polaris's minimum polar distance (A.D. 2102 Jan), with implied minimum 2M ≈ 27'29".
results.modern_name: Polaris closest approach to the north celestial pole (~2100–2102, ~27')

results.what: Statement of the biquadratic reciprocity law with supplementary terms valid for a odd, b even (either sign).
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (announced 1832); first published proofs Jacobi (lectures 1836/7), Eisenstein (1844)

deep.surprise_reason: The biquadratic law is well known as Gauss's. The precession supplement is a neat unpublished application of the half-angle (spinor/quaternion-like) representation of rotations. Gauss's 'Mutationen des Raumes' already shows he used such parameters, so the idea is not new for him. The concrete use for uniform-rotation fitting and the prediction of Polaris's closest approach in 2102 is a notable but minor detail.

checkable.sympy: s,t,m,n=symbols('s t m n',integer=True); b=2*s; B=2*t; a=1-2*s+4*m; A=1-2*t+4*n; expand(((A-1)*b+(a-1)*B+B*b)/2 - b*B/2)
checkable.asserts: Equals 4*(m*t+n*s-s*t). Gauss's form agrees mod 4 with the standard law exponent bB/2 for primary numbers.
Divisible by 4: replacing a+bi by -(a+bi) shifts the RHS by B mod 4, matching the change in character index from [-1/β]_4.

transcription_corrections: The manuscript's 4th left equation reads cos½(p−q+α) but should be cos½(p−q−α); the transcription faithfully copies the slip.
Year at end reads 'Anno 2102 Jan 18' (1815+287.0437), not 1902.
